questions.whyExplanation: Resisting mathematicians for 358 years, Fermat’s Last Theorem was finally proved by Andrew Wiles (with Richard Taylor) in 1994—uniting deep 20th-century algebraic geometry.

questions.prompt: Long dubbed "le chiffre indéchiffrable," which 16th-century cipher uses a repeating keyword to shift letters across multiple alphabets?
clues: A 26×26 tableau grid pairs each plaintext character with one letter of a secret keyword.
Babbage and Kasiski finally cracked it in the 1850s–60s using repeat spacing.
questions.whyExplanation: Actually invented by Giovan Battista Bellaso in 1553 and misattributed to diplomat Blaise de Vigenère, this polyalphabetic cipher defeated simple frequency counts for three centuries.

questions.prompt: Which 1976 computer-assisted theorem proves the exact minimum palette needed to color any flat map so no bordering regions match?
clues: Francis Guthrie first spotted this cartographic bound while coloring English counties.
Appel and Haken checked 1,834 map cases across 1,200 hours of mainframe time.
questions.whyExplanation: Proved by Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken in 1976, the Four-Color Theorem sparked fierce debate over computer-checked proofs—though on a donut-shaped torus you need seven colors!

questions.prompt: Proposed in a 1742 letter to Leonhard Euler and still unproved, what conjecture claims every even integer above 2 is the sum of two primes?
clues: Examples like 4 = 2+2, 28 = 11+17, and 100 = 47+53 hold past 4 quintillion.
Euler wrote back he was "completely certain" it was true, yet could not prove it.
questions.whyExplanation: Despite verification up to 4 × 10^18 and Harald Helfgott’s 2013 proof of the odd-number "weak" version, strong Goldbach’s Conjecture remains one of math’s oldest unsolved mysteries.

questions.prompt: What forensic-accounting law reveals that ~30.1% of naturally spanning datasets—rivers, ledgers, bills—begin with the leading digit 1?
clues: Astronomer Simon Newcomb first spotted it in 1881 because early log-table pages were grimiest!
Leading digit d appears with odds log10(1 + 1/d)—exposing forged tax books.
questions.whyExplanation: Because exponential growth spends far longer moving from 1 to 2 (+100%) than 8 to 9 (+12.5%), digit 1 leads 30.1% of real-world tables—catching clumsy accounting fraud.

questions.prompt: What 1891 Georg Cantor proof builds a new decimal digit-by-digit down a list to prove real numbers outnumber counting integers?
clues: Flipping the n-th digit of the n-th listed number guarantees the newcomer misses every row!
It proved some infinities are strictly larger ("uncountable") than integers.
questions.whyExplanation: Georg Cantor’s Diagonal Argument shattered the belief that all infinities are equal—showing the continuum of real numbers cannot be paired one-to-one with natural integers.

questions.prompt: What empirical power law observes that a language’s 2nd-most-common word occurs ~1/2 as often as the 1st, and the 3rd ~1/3 as often?
clues: Remarkably, city populations and website traffic obey the same inverse-rank 1/r curve.
Named for the Harvard linguist who charted word ranks across Joyce’s Ulysses.
questions.whyExplanation: George Zipf charted this uncanny 1/r rank law across languages and cities—even the undeciphered Voynich Manuscript obeys it, hinting at real linguistic structure.

questions.prompt: What unsolved 1937 arithmetic riddle—"halve if even, 3n + 1 if odd"—predicts every positive integer eventually collapses down to 1?
clues: Starting from 27 shoots up to 9,232 before plummeting in 111 steps down to the 4-2-1 loop.
Paul Erdős joked "mathematics may not be ready for such problems" and offered $500.
questions.whyExplanation: Verified by computers past 2^68 without a single counterexample yet still unproved, the 3n+1 "hailstone" sequence shows how one elementary rule can generate chaotic mathematical depth.

questions.prompt: What 1924 Axiom-of-Choice theorem proves a solid 3D sphere can be split into five abstract sets and rotated into TWO identical spheres?
clues: It fails for physical gold because its non-measurable pieces are infinitely fine dust.
Two Polish mathematicians published this sphere-doubling theorem in 1924.
questions.whyExplanation: Stefan Banach and Alfred Tarski proved the Axiom of Choice creates non-measurable sets lacking defined volume—letting rigid rotations duplicate an abstract 3D ball.

questions.prompt: What is the exact sum of every consecutive whole number from 1 through 100 (1 + 2 + 3 + ... + 100)?
clues: Pair the opposite ends: 1+100=101, 2+99=101—you form fifty identical 101-sum pairs.
Multiply 50 × 101 using young Carl Friedrich Gauss’s legendary classroom trick.
questions.whyExplanation: Using the triangular sum formula n(n + 1)/2, fifty matched pairs of 101 total exactly 5,050—reportedly solved in seconds by 8-year-old Carl Friedrich Gauss to his teacher’s shock.

questions.prompt: Ten diplomats enter a summit hall and every envoy shakes hands with every other envoy exactly once. How many total handshakes occur?
clues: Each of the 10 people shakes 9 hands—then divide by 2 so you don’t double-count pairs!
Equivalently, add 9 + 8 + 7 + 6 + 5 + 4 + 3 + 2 + 1.
questions.whyExplanation: A classic complete-graph K10 count: C(10, 2) = (10 × 9)/2 = 45 unique pairwise handshakes—the exact same math behind round-robin sports schedules and peer-to-peer network links.

questions.prompt: Using the Sieve of Eratosthenes, how many prime numbers exist strictly between 1 and 100?
clues: Remember 1 is NOT prime, 2 IS prime, and tricky 91 equals 7 × 13!
Exactly one-quarter of the first hundred positive integers survive the sieve.
questions.whyExplanation: From 2 up to 97, exactly 25 primes live below 100 (a clean 25% density)—after which primes thin out logarithmically near 1 / ln(n) according to the Prime Number Theorem.

questions.prompt: In the classic three-peg Tower of Hanoi puzzle, what is the minimum number of single-disk moves required to relocate a stack of 7 disks?
clues: Each extra disk doubles the previous moves and adds 1—yielding the formula (2^n) − 1.
Take two to the seventh power (128) and subtract one.
questions.whyExplanation: Invented by Édouard Lucas in 1883, transferring n disks takes exactly 2^n − 1 moves: 7 disks need 127 moves, while Lucas’s mythical 64-disk golden tower would take 585 billion years!

questions.prompt: How many straight edges connect the 20 triangular faces and 12 vertices of a regular icosahedron (a standard 20-sided gaming die)?
clues: Plug V = 12 and F = 20 into Euler’s convex polyhedron rule: V − E + F = 2.
Or multiply 20 faces × 3 sides and halve it since each edge joins two faces.
questions.whyExplanation: Both Euler’s formula (12 − E + 20 = 2) and half-edge counting (20 × 3 / 2) give exactly 30 edges—the same edge count shared with its geometric dual, the 12-faced dodecahedron.

questions.prompt: What Hardy-Ramanujan "taxicab number" is the smallest positive integer expressible as a sum of two positive cubes in two distinct ways?
clues: G. H. Hardy rode this numbered London cab to visit Srinivasa Ramanujan and called it dull.
Add nine cubed to ten cubed—the exact same total as one cubed plus twelve cubed!
questions.whyExplanation: Ramanujan instantly replied that 1,729 is fascinating: 1³ + 12³ = 1 + 1,728 and 9³ + 10³ = 729 + 1,000—making it Ta(2), and remarkably it is also the third Carmichael pseudoprime!

questions.prompt: Match each two-input Boolean logic gate to the exact condition that outputs 1 (TRUE).
clues: Both Inputs 0 defines a NOR gate—leaving it out as the lower-ring decoy.
Exclusive-OR (XOR) fires strictly when one input is 1 and the other is 0.
questions.whyExplanation: Boolean gates convert George Boole’s 1854 algebra into silicon switches: AND requires both 1s, OR accepts either or both, and XOR lights up only when the two bits disagree.

questions.prompt: Pair each classic debate fallacy with the exact reasoning flaw it commits.
clues: Appeals to Emotion defines ad misericordiam—making it the unaligned decoy.
Post Hoc mistakes sequence for cause; Tu Quoque ("you too") deflects with hypocrisy.
questions.whyExplanation: Spotting rhetorical traps sharpens deduction: post hoc assumes "after means caused by," tu quoque dodges critique via "whataboutism," and circular logic presupposes its own proof.

questions.prompt: Align each literary or cryptic wordplay device with its matching textbook example.
clues: Radar Spelled Back illustrates a palindrome—leaving it out as the decoy.
Georges Perec wrote a 300-page lipogram novel ("A Void") without a single E!
questions.whyExplanation: Lewis Carroll popularized "portmanteau" for suitcase-blended words like smog, oxymorons fuse opposites like "deafening silence," and lipograms ban a chosen letter entirely.

questions.prompt: Match each distinguished mathematical integer class to its strictly unique example below.
clues: 27 is simply 3 cubed—making it the unaligned decoy on the lower ring.
Proper divisors of 28 (1+2+4+7+14) sum to 28; 31 equals (2^5) − 1; 120 equals 5!.
questions.whyExplanation: 28 is the second perfect number (after 6), 31 is the third Mersenne prime (2^5 − 1), and 120 is 5 factorial (5×4×3×2×1)—while 27 belongs to none of those three classes.

questions.prompt: In standard real-number arithmetic, the infinitely repeating decimal 0.999... is strictly less than 1 by a microscopic gap.
clues: Take 1/3 = 0.333... and multiply both sides cleanly by 3!
In real numbers zero gap fits between them: 0.999... and 1 are IDENTICAL.
questions.whyExplanation: Famous math myth! Setting x = 0.999... gives 10x − x = 9, so x = 1; in the real numbers ℝ, no number fits between 0.999... and 1, proving exact equality.

questions.prompt: By universal mathematical convention, zero factorial (0!) evaluates to exactly 1 rather than 0.
clues: How many ways can you arrange zero books on an empty shelf? Exactly ONE way—leave it empty!
It also preserves n! = n × (n − 1)! when n = 1, plus combinations like C(n, n) = 1.
questions.whyExplanation: True! Setting 0! = 1 (the empty product) keeps factorial recurrence n! = n·(n−1)!, Taylor series, binomial coefficients, and Euler’s Gamma function Γ(1) = 1 seamlessly consistent.

questions.prompt: Because 1 divides evenly only by itself and 1, modern mathematics classifies 1 as the very smallest prime number.
clues: A prime integer must have strictly TWO distinct positive divisors—1 has only one!
Allowing 1 as prime would break unique prime factorization (6 = 2×3 = 1×1×2×3).
questions.whyExplanation: False! Modern number theory excludes 1 so every integer above 1 factors into primes in strictly one unique way—preserving the Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic.

questions.prompt: If two real-world variables maintain a 99 percent positive statistical correlation over decades, one must directly cause the other.
clues: Summer ice-cream sales and swimming drownings track tightly—yet cones don’t cause drownings!
A hidden third variable (like summer heat) or shared trend drives false links.
questions.whyExplanation: Classic cum hoc fallacy! Even r = 0.99 never proves direct causation alone—hidden confounders, reverse causality, and shared time trends fool analysts constantly.

questions.prompt: There are more possible ways to order a shuffled 52-card playing deck (52!) than there are atoms making up the entire planet Earth.
clues: Earth contains roughly 10^50 atoms—now compare that against 52 × 51 × 50 × ... × 1!
52! tops 8 × 10^67—beating Earth’s atom count by 17 full orders of magnitude.
questions.whyExplanation: True! 52! ≈ 8.07 × 10^67 dwarfs Earth’s ~1.3 × 10^50 atoms by more than 10^17 times—meaning every thoroughly shuffled deck you hold has almost certainly never existed before in history.

questions.prompt: The deductive argument "If it rains, the street is wet; the street is wet; therefore it rained" is formally valid.
clues: Could a street sweeper or burst water main soak the pavement under a cloudless blue sky?
Leaping from "P → Q" and "Q" back to "P" commits affirming the consequent.
questions.whyExplanation: False! That is the textbook formal fallacy of affirming the consequent; valid logic requires confirming rain (modus ponens) or observing a dry street (modus tollens).
